meta.title: Who really said "Experience is a brutal teacher, but you learn. My God, do you learn"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not C.S. Lewis. This line was written by screenwriter William Nicholson for the 1993 film Shadowlands and spoken by Anthony Hopkins — not found in Lewis's writings.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Experience is a brutal teacher, but you learn. My God, do you learn'?
meta.ogDescription: Not C.S. Lewis. It was written by William Nicholson for the film Shadowlands (1993) and spoken by Anthony Hopkins as Lewis. It appears in none of Lewis's books.

answer.label: Not C.S. Lewis — actually screenwriter William Nicholson
answer.sourceLine: This is film dialogue, not something Lewis wrote. William Nicholson penned the line for his screenplay Shadowlands, and Anthony Hopkins delivers it on screen as Lewis in the 1993 film — where it runs roughly “Experience: that most brutal of teachers. But you learn, my God do you learn.” The popular one-line wording is a lightly reworded paraphrase of that movie line, and it appears in none of Lewis’s published works ↗.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from
source.excerpt: Experience: that most brutal of teachers. But you learn, my God do you learn.
trail: The official CSLewis.com “Surprised By Misquotes” page ↗ states the line is “actually misquoting the movie line from Shadowlands written by William Nicholson,” delivered on screen by Anthony Hopkins.
The scholarly Essential C.S. Lewis analysis ↗ confirms the line originates in the 1993 film and is “NOT found in the published writings of Lewis.”
The Wikiquote discussion page ↗ notes no reliable source has ever tied the line to Lewis himself, with the Shadowlands film as the best lead.
Shadowlands (1993) ↗ is a biographical drama with a screenplay by William Nicholson and Anthony Hopkins as C.S. Lewis.
source.cutTag: the film line vs. the internet paraphrase
source.excerptNote: The line as spoken by Anthony Hopkins (as C.S. Lewis) in the film Shadowlands. The widely circulated “Experience is a brutal teacher, but you learn. My God, do you learn” is a reworded paraphrase of this dialogue.
source.rightsHolder: William Nicholson and the producers of Shadowlands
source.rightsNote: The line is dialogue from Shadowlands, a work first produced in the 1980s–90s (TV 1985, stage 1989, film 1993) — decades after 1931 — so it is firmly in copyright, held by screenwriter William Nicholson and the film’s producers. It is not a public-domain quotation of C.S. Lewis.

author.name: William Nicholson
author.heading: Written for the screen, not the page
author.bio: William Nicholson is an English screenwriter, playwright and novelist, born in 1948. He created Shadowlands — first a 1985 BBC television film, then a 1989 stage play, then the 1993 feature film directed by Richard Attenborough — a dramatization of C.S. Lewis's marriage to Joy Davidman and her death. His screenwriting credits also include Gladiator and Les Misérables (2012). The “brutal teacher” line is his invention, written for Hopkins's Lewis, not a quotation of the real Lewis.

misattribution.heading: How Lewis got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a classic case of a fictional character's words being mistaken for the real person's. Because Anthony Hopkins delivers the line while portraying C.S. Lewis, the quotation migrated online under Lewis's name.

items.why: The line appears in none of Lewis's published works ↗; it was written for the screen, not by Lewis.
Per the official CSLewis.com misquotes page ↗, the words were written by William Nicholson for Shadowlands and spoken by Anthony Hopkins.

items.who: Tim Allen's character on Last Man Standing
items.why: Both the CSLewis.com and Essential C.S. Lewis ↗ write-ups note a 2017 Last Man Standing episode credited the line to Lewis, spreading the mistake further.

misattribution.truthLine: The words belong to screenwriter William Nicholson's Shadowlands, spoken by an actor playing Lewis — not to C.S. Lewis himself ↗.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Shadowlands dramatizes the real grief C.S. Lewis felt after the death of his wife, Joy Davidman. Nicholson gave the on-screen Lewis this aphorism about experience — and because the sentiment fits the real man's reflective, plainspoken voice, readers rarely question it.

That plausibility is exactly what makes it durable. It sounds like Lewis, it is spoken by a beloved actor playing Lewis, and so it spreads across quote sites under his name even though he never wrote it.
context.pull: It sounds like Lewis because it was written to be spoken as Lewis.
